name: Gravitational Field Concepts
what: This subtopic covers the definition of a gravitational field as a vector field, the distinction between uniform and non-uniform fields, and how gravitational fields are represented using field lines. It also covers the nature of mass as a gravitational monopole.
why: Understanding gravitational fields is the foundation for all further work in this topic. The field model allows us to explain how masses exert forces on each other at a distance, and it forms the basis for understanding satellite motion and gravitational potential energy.

items.title: I can describe what a gravitational field is and why it is classified as a vector field
items.what: A gravitational field is a region of space where an object with mass experiences a gravitational force. It is a vector field because at every point in space it has both a magnitude (field strength) and a direction.
items.why: Classifying the gravitational field as a vector field distinguishes it from scalar fields and allows us to represent it using arrows that show both strength and direction, which is essential for solving problems involving forces.
items.example: At a point 1000 km above Earth's surface, the gravitational field has a specific magnitude of approximately 7.3 N kg⁻¹ and is directed towards the centre of Earth. Both pieces of information are needed to fully describe the field at that point.

items.title: I can draw and interpret gravitational field line diagrams for a spherical mass
items.what: Gravitational field lines point radially inward toward the centre of a spherical mass. Lines that are closer together indicate a stronger field, and lines further apart indicate a weaker field. Field lines never cross each other.
items.why: Field line diagrams give a visual representation of how the strength and direction of gravity varies in space around a mass. Interpreting these diagrams is a required skill for both theory and exam questions.
items.example: For a diagram of Earth as a spherical mass, field lines would be drawn as arrows pointing inward from all directions toward Earth's centre. The arrows would be more densely packed close to Earth's surface and more spread out at greater distances.

items.title: I can explain why mass is described as a gravitational monopole, not a dipole
items.what: A monopole is either a pure source (field lines point outward) or a pure sink (field lines point inward). Mass is always a gravitational monopole because gravity is always attractive, so field lines always point inward toward the mass. A dipole has both a source and a sink paired together.
items.why: Understanding that gravity only attracts (never repels) explains the monopole nature of mass and distinguishes gravitational fields from magnetic and electric fields, which can form dipoles.
items.example: A bar magnet is a dipole because it has a north pole (field lines emerging) and a south pole (field lines entering). A planet like Mars has no equivalent repulsive end — its gravitational field lines all point inward, making it a monopole.

items.title: I can distinguish between uniform and non-uniform gravitational fields
items.what: A uniform gravitational field has constant strength and direction at all points, represented by evenly spaced parallel field lines. A non-uniform field varies in strength and direction, represented by field lines that are more densely packed in some regions than others.
items.why: This distinction determines which formulas and methods can be used. The formula Eg = mgΔh only applies in uniform fields, while non-uniform fields require the inverse square law or graphical methods.
items.example: Close to Earth's surface, the gravitational field can be approximated as uniform at 9.8 N kg⁻¹ downward — the field lines are approximately parallel. Further from Earth, the field is non-uniform: at 408 km altitude (the ISS), the field strength has decreased to 8.67 N kg⁻¹.

items.title: I can identify gravitational fields as static fields
items.what: A static field does not change over time, as opposed to a changing field that varies with time. The gravitational field around a planet is static because the mass of the planet does not change appreciably over human timescales.
items.why: Identifying whether a field is static or changing is a required classification skill in the study design and determines how the field must be modelled.
items.example: The gravitational field around Earth is considered static for calculations involving satellites and projectiles. In contrast, an electromagnetic wave involves a changing electric and magnetic field.
